rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods <U+2013> split-plot field experiment at KARE, 1.4 ha pomegranate orchard, SDI vs DI main plots with 3 N sub-treatments, 5 replicates, 2013<U+2013>2015. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 3 <U+2013> in 2013 prime and subprime fruit weights differed statistically between SDI and DI (SDI higher prime); in 2015 subprime yield differed between DI and SDI; total yield never statistically different.
rows.notes: Single method (harvest yield per plot); one site, one soil (Hanford sandy loam), one cultivar; plot scale. Mechanism (N placement in root zone, lower weeds) asserted rather than tested as the pathway to yield; leaf N and soil nitrate were measured but not linked analytically to the yield difference. Yield tables give means with letter groupings only; 95% CIs mentioned in methods but not reported for yield. No limitation stated for the yield comparison itself.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods <U+2013> own field experiment (SDI vs DI, split plot, 5 replicates). Q2: Section 3.7 and Table 8 <U+2013> residual weed biomass on 28 Aug 2013 was 81 g/m2 under SDI vs 569 g/m2 under DI, significant at P=0.0001; Fig. 8 shows the visual difference in 2012. Q8: Section 3.7 <U+2013> authors state weed mass was not measured in other growing seasons, only observed.
rows.notes: Weed biomass was quantified on a single date in one year; the infrared surface temperature correlation (R=-0.636) is a proxy co-measurement rather than an independent method establishing weed reduction, so Q3 rated no with doubt. Surface soil wetness (the presumed mechanism) was not measured; SMP sensors were at 0.6<U+2013>1.5 m in the lysimeter. Table 8 reports means and F probabilities, no dispersion.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods <U+2013> own field experiment with metered water application per system. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 4 <U+2013> WP for total yield consistently higher in SDI (60.4, 61.0, 59.7 kg/ha/mm) than DI (51.5, 53.4, 55.8), attributed by the authors to higher average SDI yields and lower applied water (843 vs 932 mm in 2015, Table 1).
rows.notes: The lower water application to SDI was imposed by design (DI deliberately given ~10% more to cover surface evaporation and weed use), not measured as a saving; soil evaporation was not measured. WP by irrigation system was not statistically tested and no dispersion reported. Only generic 'additional study required' on further SDI reductions.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods <U+2013> own split-plot field experiment. Q2: Section 3.4, Table 3 and Conclusions <U+2013> average yield was consistently higher under SDI than DI in all three years (e.g. prime yield 40,917 vs 33,748 kg/ha in 2015), though total yields were not statistically different.
rows.notes: Yield difference between SDI and DI not statistically significant for total yield; significant only for prime/subprime categories in some years. Single site, soil and cultivar; plot scale; means with letter groups only; mechanism asserted (N placement near roots) not tested as the pathway.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods <U+2013> own field experiment, water applications metered. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 4 <U+2013> water productivity consistently higher for SDI than DI in 2013<U+2013>2015 because of higher SDI yields and lower applied water (SDI 843 mm vs DI 932 mm in 2015).
rows.notes: Applied-water difference was set by design (10% extra to DI), so the WUE advantage is partly an assumption built into the treatment; no statistical test or dispersion for WP by irrigation system; one site/soil/crop; plot scale.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods <U+2013> own field experiment. Q2: Section 3.7, Table 8 <U+2013> weed biomass significantly lower under SDI (81 g/m2) than DI (569 g/m2), P=0.0001, measured 28 Aug 2013. Q8: Section 3.7 <U+2013> weed mass not measured in other seasons, only observed to be consistently greater in DI.
rows.notes: Single sampling date in one year; IR surface temperature correlation treated as a proxy, not an independent method; surface soil moisture mechanism not measured; no dispersion reported in Table 8.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods <U+2013> own split-plot field experiment. Q2: Section 3.4, Tables 3, 4 and 6 and Conclusions <U+2013> average yield consistently higher in SDI than DI (not statistically different for total yield); WP consistently higher in SDI; N productivity higher in SDI in 2013 and 2014.
rows.notes: Higher yield under SDI is a consistent but non-significant difference; NP advantage absent in 2015. Single site, soil and cultivar; plot scale; means with letter groups only, no dispersion for yield or productivity by irrigation system; mechanism asserted not tested.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a single-site field trial (Hanford sandy loam, KARE, California) of SDI vs DI pomegranate with three N rates, 2013<U+2013>2015; drainage/leaching results come from a single SDI-irrigated lysimeter tree. Statistical 95% CIs are mentioned in methods but reported only as SE bars for leaf/fruit N figures, not for yield, WP or weed biomass.
